Elimination of natural drainage from the forested Bad and West Bad Creek drainage would remove a large area now contributing to the productivity of the aquatic food web downstream in Howard Creek. Flooding the Bad Creek drainage and operating of the generating facilities would permit some leaching nutrients that could contribute to the productivity of Lake Jocassee, although the extent of this contribution cannot be predicted.
Inundation of Bad Creek and West Bad Creek would result in the loss of 2.3 miles and 1.3 acres of trout water, representing an estimated 68 hours of angling and 30 to 40 fishing trips. This would mean an annual loss in fishing benefits ranging from $189 to $252, at an assumed value of $6.30/day (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 1970). More recent published estimates for the monetary value of fishing range from $13.90 to $160.36, with an average value of $32.30 (Horvath, 1974). Using the latter figure, this would place the annual loss in fishing benefits within the proposed impoundment area at between $969 and $1,292. Horvath also rates the average daily value lost by giving up a day of fresh-coldwater fishing in natural rivers. The rating of $18.97 was listed as the average daily worth of fishing, while $30.28 was the average daily amount a fisherman required to give up this category of recreation. Projecting the estimated 30 to 40 fishing trips in the project impoundment area for each of these two values would mean a potential recreational fishing loss of between $569 to $769 and $908 to $1,211.20, respectively.
In the normal operation of the proposed project, the reservoir would experience the extreme conditions of rapid drawdown. The reservoir side slopes, being very steep and unstable, could cause a high degree of bank sloughing and slope wash in the initial period of operation. Runoff from exposed land areas above the full-pool elevation would also occur. Nutrients, some organic matter, and soluble solids could be leached from the reservoir banks. Alteration of pH could also occur. These factors could affect the use of this water for flow augmentation and would be transmitted into Lake Jocassee during generation. Turbidity would be increased locally near the outlet structure in Lage Jocassee. After the first few seasons of operation, this condition should stabilize and a somewhat permanent shoreline would result. Due to the granular nature of the soils, it is not expected that turbidity of the reservoir waters would be a prolonged or lasting condition.
